newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia looks anew at Tenaga, plays down IPPs.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia looks anew at Tenaga, plays down IPPs.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Thursday his confidence had been restored in state power utility Tenaga Nasional Bhd after an embarrassing nationwide blackout in August.
"I'm as confident as I can be," Mahathir told reporters after making his first official visit to Tenaga's premises in six years.
He attended a briefing on the progress of the company by chairman Ahmad Tajuddin Ali, who was appointed following the power outage.

Mahathir said Tenaga's role as an electricity provider will be developed and major contracts would no longer be granted by the government to private power companies known as Independent Power Producers (IPPs).
For instance, a newly-approved 2,000 MW power project in Perak state will be built by Tenaga and not an IPP, he said.
"We have stopped giving to the IPPs now because I think it's Tenaga's turn to expand," Mahathir said. "For now...there'll be no major opportunities for IPPs."
"But they (Tenaga) will have to be given time. They can't give an absolute guarantee that there will be no blackouts in future, but can guarantee the risks will be minimal," he added.
Mahathir's conciliatory remarks came after he criticised the utility for a 15-hour blackout on August 3 which left peninsular Malaysia in darkness and cost businesses millions of dollars.

The blackout was the second nationwide outage in four years. Tenaga, which is 70 percent owned by the government, came under fire for a 10-day outage in Penang island in June 1995. The northern state is the hub of the country's electronics industry.

Officials at Tenaga said that since the August blackout, the government has appeared to be more concerned about the company's complaint that it was overpaying for electricity it had agreed to buy from IPPs.
There are five IPPs in Malaysia, all licensed in 1993 after the country's power reserves were found to be below demand at peak hours.
Officials said Malaysia now had more than 40 percent excess power capacity and that Tenaga's payments to IPPs comprised about 40 percent of its operating costs last year.
Mahathir said the government was planning to ask IPPs to contribute towards the cost of providing power to rural areas. Tenaga has borne such costs in the past.
"But we will need to hear from them (the IPPs) first," he said.
Ahmad Jauhari Yahya, honorary president of the Association of IPPs, was quoted as saying by the New Straits Times on Thursday that he was open to the plan.
